CHAPTER 2 VISION, PRINCIPLES AND BASIS OF THE PLAN
2.1 CITY OF WATERLOO COMMUNITY VISION STATEMENT
This Official Plan is based on achieving the following community vision statement:
In
2051
, the City of Waterloo
is
a green
resilient and low carbon
c
ity
with healthy green
spaces, land, water and clean air;
well
-
designed in accordance with local urban design
objectives
;
an economic leader with a strong diverse economy; a
n inclusive
community
of vibrant neighbourhoods and a range of housing options; a learning community with
strong ties to its schools, universities and college; an exciting
c
ity with abundant
recreation, leisure, arts and cultural opportunities; and a
c
ity
that is accessib
le to all.
2.2 PRINCIP
L
ES OF THE PLA
N
Achievement of the vision is guided by a set of principles that draw from the pillars of
sustainability. These principles form the foundation
of
the objectives and policies found in
subsequent chapters of this Plan.
(1) Environmental Sustainability
An environmentally sustainable city is one that supports a healthy urban and natural
environment, both within and beyond its borders, is resilient to the impacts of climate
change, makes efficient use of resources and green
infrastructure
, and supports low
-
carbon practices such as local clean energy production, reduced energy consumption,
active transportation
and public transit. This Plan recognizes the important role that
built form, building design, transportation
infrastructure
and natural and public
sp
aces play in safeguarding human and ecosystem health, and supporting choices
that will help Waterloo transition to a low carbon community.
(2) Equity and Inclusion
An equitable and inclusive city offers people of all ages, abilities, incomes and
backgrounds and equity
-
deserving groups, a high quality of life, health and wellness,
feeling of safety and a sense of belonging. An equitable city offers public and private
spaces and amenities that acknowledge the cultural heritage of the past and support
the cultural practices of the present. This Plan acknowledges Indigenous heritage and
takes steps to support truth and reconciliation in planning and planning processes. It
also strives to meet the needs of our growing and diversifying population by
supporting equitable access to and a diversity of options for housing, transportation,
employment, and amenities. The Plan provides policies to guide planning and design
of inclu
sive, vibrant, and accessible public realm
s
and developments that foster social
interaction.

7
(3) Economic Sustainability
An economically sustainable city supports opportunities for employment, investment,
talent attraction and retention,
affordable
and accessible housing, and plans for the
long term and life
-
cycle costs of growth and supporting
infrastructure
and services.
This Plan provides direction for the efficient and cost
-
effective use of land and
infrastructure
, opportunities for employment, commercial and academic growth, and
an increased supply and diversity of housing, including
affordable
housing, to support
the co
mmunity’s prosperity, competitiveness and resilience, provided other City
objectives related to complete communities, built form
and urban design are achieved.
2.3
BASIS OF THE PLAN
The development of this Plan has been based on an understanding of the local and broader
context as well as anticipated trends and factors that may have an influence on growth and
change in Waterloo. The purpose of this
s
ection is to provide an overview of trends and
factors that are considered to have a significant influence on the land use policies and
designations of this Plan. The overview relates to,
and should be read in conjunction with the
remaining chapters of this Plan
.
Growth and City Form
(1)
There is a limited supply of vacant land for future urban growth. To ensure that
population and economic growth can be
accommodated;
land within the City must be
used more efficiently.
Most
of the City’s population and employment growt
h
will
be
accommodated through
intensification
within the existing
Urban
Area. Focal points
for
intensification
include the Uptown Waterloo
Primary Node
,
Major Transit Station
Areas
and other designated Nodes and Corridors.
Areas outside of priority growth
areas will be planne
d to accommodate some growth through context
-
sensitive
intensification
.
(2)
Uptown Waterloo is a focal point within the City, and forms Waterloo’s Primary Node.
The Uptown Waterloo Primary Node will be planned to permit cultural facilities,
recreational uses, institutional uses, public open spaces, residential, employment and
comm
ercial uses that collectively create a vibrant, human
-
scaled Uptown Waterloo
area. This form of growth will support transit and
active transportation
modes, reduce
the need for automobile travel and commuting times to and from the Uptown
Waterloo area, and
support a
pedestrian
-
oriented streetscape.
(3)
The policies in this Plan support public transit investments by focusing
intensification
within designated Major Transit Station Areas, the Uptown Waterloo Primary Node,
and designated Nodes and Corridors. These areas will be planned to support existing
and planned transit service levels and will accommodate
Transit Oriented

8
Development
.
(4)
Waterloo will be planned
to support
complete communit
ies
that provide
s
opportunities for people at all stages of life
, incomes and abilities
to live, work, learn,
shop, and play in close proximity. Planning for compact,
mixed
-
use
communities helps
to reduce
infrastructure
and service duplication costs, preserves rural lands,
encourages
a diversity of housing options,
social interaction and a greater sense of
community, supports
active
transportation
and transit
, and reduces travel needs and
commuting times.
(5)
A high standard of urban design supports a
memorable
, attractive, and livable city. To
achieve this, policies of this Plan define key urban design elements to be applied
generally across the City and more specifically within the Uptown Waterloo
Primary
Node, Major Transit Station Areas,
and other designated Nodes and Corridors.
Networks and Transportation
(6)
Active forms of transportation provide alternatives to the automobile and this Plan
places a high priority on encouraging
active transportation
. Objectives and policies in
this Plan recognize the strong relationship between transportation and land use by
planning for a transportation network that supports designated Nodes and Corridors
and their planned
intensification
, thereby providing people with the opportunity to live
closer to where they work, learn, shop and play.
(7)
It is desirable to plan for and support a shift in focus from providing
roads
to move
cars, to providing streets where people can interact and travel on, whether by foot,
bicycle, transit or other motorized vehicle.
Roads
under the City’s jurisdiction will be
planned to serve as a network of
complete streets
, facilitating the movement of, and
interaction between, all travel modes
–
pedestrians
, bicycles, transit and motorized
vehicles
–
within and throughout the City. The
complete streets
concept recognizes
that the streets within the road network provide meeting places for social and
business interaction and as such, need to provide access for a full range of
residents
within the community.
(8)
Bicycle and vehicular parking are an integral component of the City’s transportation
system. Policies outline the City’s expectations regarding the design and development
of future parking areas to meet community needs and seek to ensure that parking
areas
balance the needs of motorists with the needs of users of active travel modes
such as walking, cycling
, or rolling
.
(9)
The City will plan for the extension or expansion of existing services to ensure
contiguous growth, minimize the under
-
utilization of municipal services and to
support the achievement of minimum
intensification
targets within
developed areas
.
Where it is determined that adequate municipal water, sanitary or storm sewer

9
capacity does not exist to support proposed development, the City shall not be
obligated to provide such services in advance of available budget resources.
(10)
The City will plan for trails and open space networks and supporting facilities that are
interconnected and serve transportation, recreation and leisure, and environmental
functions.
City Liveability
(11)
Healthy social and cultural systems contribute to a healthy, sustainable and
economically vibrant community. This Plan also recognizes the importance of
planning for the provision of a wide range of arts, culture, heritage, recreation and
leisure facilitie
s, programs and services to meet the needs and contribute to the future
quality of life of the community.
(12)
The City will pl
a
n to maximize
t
he use of exi
s
ting faciliti
e
s and community resources
in the provision of arts, c
u
lture, heritage, r
e
creation and leisure facilities, services and
programs.
(13)
In acknowledgment of the expanded powers and responsibilities provided to
municipalities by the Province of Ontario, the
conservation
of
cultural
heritage
resources
is required. The Heritage policies of this Plan provide a detailed framework
for
conservation
of the City’s
cultural heritage resources
.
Economy
(14)
T
his Plan contains policies that recognize Waterloo’s diverse economy and protect
Waterloo’s
employment
areas from conversion to non
-
employment uses
in accordance
with the Provincial Planning Statement
and the City’s planning objectives for
employment
in this Plan
.
(15)
Creative, sustainable cities are supported by strong and interconnected social,
cultural, economic and environmental systems. This Plan seeks to strengthen
relationships between these systems, and recognizes that creative, sustainable cities
will be compet
itive in the knowledge economy. This Plan recognizes that the City will
play an active role in ensuring that Waterloo displays characteristics of a creative and
sustainable city.
(16)
P
lace a continued emphasis on collaboration and sharing of information and ideas
between business, government and non
-
government organizations on issues of
shared interest, including economic issues.
(17)
Research, academic, and other learning institutions are an important element of
Waterloo’s economy. Policies provide support for growth in research institutions and
think tank clusters and recognize the planned growth of the three post
-
secondary

10
educational institutions. The role of libraries is recognized in terms of facilitating
access to information and lifelong learning opportunities.
Environment and Energy
(18)
A healthy, diverse environment is a pillar for a healthy, sustainable community.
Policies are intended to protect significant environmental features and functions from
development
and
site alteration
that will have an
adverse environmental impact
.
(19)
The supply and efficient use of energy is critically important to the future of all
residents, businesses and other institutions within Waterloo. Policies in the Plan
encourage the efficient use of energy resources through community and site design
as well
as building techniques designed to conserve energy.
